title: woww: Auto generate implementation from wowm
description:
Progresses #17481.

This PR auto generates the Wireshark definitions from the `wowm` files at [the wow_messages repo](https://github.com/gtker/wow_messages/tree/main/wow_message_parser/wowm/world). `wowm` is a DSL I'm working on that is also used for generating a library and documentation. The auto generator for Wireshark [is located in the same repo](https://github.com/gtker/wow_messages/tree/main/wow_message_parser/src/wireshark_printer).

I tried to split it into distinct commits that still compile and run correctly.

I realize that just dumping a gazillion LOC on you isn't very fun, but the alternative of creating smaller PRs over weeks/months would probably just stretch out the pain for everybody involved. There are 607 distinct messages, so even adding 20 per week would still take over half a year, and it would require reviewers to review 30 PRs that are really just the same thing. This would also just unnecessarily slow down the rate at which people got a useful dissector and add a significant administrative burden on everybody involved.

Autogenerating the defintions has significant benefits since updates to the `wowm` DSL will automatically update the docs, libraries and wireshark dissector without any additional information. Trying to use the wireshark implementation for debugging was pretty severely hampered by having message definitions not match the wireshark definitions, which led to significant pain.

Future work will include:
* better and more accurate `wowm` definitions.
* deduplication of identical cases.
* Support for 2.4.3 and 3.3.5 as originally discussed in #11398. This is now possible since I don't have to manually implement everything myself but can use community additions from the `wowm` definitions.

The support for 2.4.3 is relatively easy, since the header deduction is functionally the same as for 1.12.
3.3.5 changes the header encryption system to use RC4. I believe it is possible to crack the cipher in a useful time frame because of vulnerabilities discovered in RC4 and knowledge of the data being encrypted.

Let me know if you want any changes. :)

Note the way that you hardcode the port, even the preference is changed, 8085 is always used to determine whether a packet is server or client. Is that what you want, or is it possible to have a server port other than 8085? If so, you can look at what the TFTP dissector, the Quake dissectors, among others, do with `value_is_in_range()` to test to see whether the destination or source port is the one that matched in order to guess whether something is server or client. (Assuming that the port set to the preference is server, and the client port is ephemeral.)

I have changed the server/client detection to depend on which port is lesser. I know this isn't a guaranteed  thing but I'm not sure what else to do without some analysis.

I'm considering detecting whether a port sends an `SMSG` (Server Message, from the server) and then logically it must be the server, but this will have to come in a future PR.

> This would regress #17720.
> 
> Port 8085 is not IANA registered to WOWW, and is commonly used by web servers.

In particular, do *NOT* do this:

    dissector_add_uint_with_preference("tcp.port", WOWW_TCP_PORT, woww_handle);

Instead, do something such as

    dissector_add_for_decode_as("tcp.port", woww_handle);

so that the user can cause a particular port to be decoded as WoWW.

If you can develop a heuristic that, by looking at the packet contents, can reasonably accurately guess whether a packet is WoWW or not, you could make the dissector heuristic and register it as a heuristic dissector for TCP payloads.

> Instead, do something such as

Thanks, I'll take a look. I was really just copy pasting from the WOW protocol which did the same thing so I didn't even know that this was the wrong way of doing it.
Changed to `dissector_add_for_decode_as` instead. Heuristics will come in a later PR since it aligns with the 2.4.3 and 3.3.5 support I'm planning.

If I understand correctly, it would be possible to develop a heuristic that would work for the initial unencrypted packets, which have a fixed 4 bytes, depending on direction (either the first 4 bytes for SMSG AUTH CHALLENGE or the 4 bytes of the opcode after the length in CMSG_AUTH_SESSION.) That is low enough probability that heuristics are reasonable. If either of those packets are encountered, return TRUE. (Note that the WOW_MIN_LENGTH test needs to be different for the client packets vs server packets; you should reject packets less than 6 bytes in the one direction because throwing an exception in a heuristic is unacceptable.)

On the other hand, it is difficult to create a heuristic determine from a single encrypted packet that it is WOWW. So a heuristic that works for the unencrypted packets and otherwise does Decode As as Guy suggests would be a natural approach.

I suppose that you could implement a heuristic that saves state for a conversation. After trying a number of packets you could determine that you're getting inconsistent values for the session key and thus it's not actually WOWW and return FALSE from then on without further tests, and conversely after processing enough packets could be very confident that it is WOWW and set the conversation dissector, all the time rejecting out of caution while building up the proposed session key. I'm not sure anyone has implemented a heuristic like that for any dissector.

If I understand correctly from reading `handle_packet_header()`, you already assume that the first packet in either direction is unencrypted rather than considering that you might have a capture that starts in the middle of a connection. Are you sure you want to do that? (That would be another reason to develop a heuristic test function.)

Responding to all three comments in one.

> This would regress #17720.

Oh whoops, my bad, I was under the impression that my branch was on the current master, but it appears to have been pretty damn old.

> Is that what you want, or is it possible to have a server port other than 8085?

It is possible to have a server port that isn't 8085, but 8085 is the default.

> If so, you can look at what the TFTP dissector, the Quake dissectors, among others, do with `value_is_in_range()` to test to see whether the destination or source port is the one that matched in order to guess whether something is server or client.

Interesting, will do. Should I push it to this PR or do you want it in another one?

> If I understand correctly from reading `handle_packet_header()`, you already assume that the first packet in either direction is unencrypted rather than considering that you might have a capture that starts in the middle of a connection.

That's correct. This dissector is not really robust in any definition of the word, mostly due to me not knowing much about writing Wireshark dissectors and also kind of discovering the format of WOWW while I go.

If I return `FALSE` from the dissector once, can I then be guaranteed that the dissector won't be called again unless the user specifically asks for it?

> If I return FALSE from the dissector once, can I then be guaranteed that the dissector won't be called again unless the user specifically asks for it?

Not necessarily. If your heuristic return FALSE and some other heuristic sets itself as the dissector for the conversation, the other dissector will be called. But if no heuristic dissector sets itself as the dissectors for the conversation, then your dissector could get called on a later packet.

For the same reason, once you know that your protocol is the correct one, it's good to use 'conversation_set_dissector' for a heuristic dissector. There's some documentation in the doc/ directory in the source tree on how to write a heuristic dissector.

Some dissectors do return TRUE but don't claim all future packets on the same port - one case where you want to do that is how STUN and RTP often multiplex on the same UDP 5-tuple.

That so many protocols use unregistered ports make it difficult to write something that works not just on captures with your protocol, but also avoids false positives.

> If your heuristic return FALSE and some other heuristic sets itself as the dissector for the conversation, the other dissector will be called.

Alright, I'll take a look.

My next PR is going to do some "analysis" of the initial messages anyway to select between 1.12 and 2.4.3, would it be OK if I got this merged now and waited until the next PR with the heuristics?
can you add also a note on docbook/release-note about "new" dissector ?
Sure, although this dissector isn't new. I believe the patch notes back then was just something like "added too many dissectors to mention" or something, but I'll add it now.
a note about some rework the dissector (may be some display filter change ?)
Added more explanatory text in the same section because I couldn't really see where else it would fit in.

Fixed with the latest commit. Is there any easy way to know this without digging into the CI artifacts and searching for `woww`?
There is on artifacts, some files with only file changed on this MR (or you can look raw log, there is a 'tee' of this log...) (for Clang Analysis Build step)

Ah, alright.

In `item_calls_check.txt` I see a bunch of warnings. I'll get rid of the `called consecutively`, but how do you want me to handle the (for example) `hf_woww_item_quality  -  item type is FT_UINT8 but call has len 4` where `hf_woww_item_quality` is a single byte sized enum that just happens to be sent as a four byte size int? In all these cases the value is never larger than a byte.

The developers were not really consistent with many of the field sizes.

it is a tools from @cjmaynard it is not a "major" warning can be ignore

(on you code, the length is 4 for this field only one time it is only 1 octet length)

Ah, OK, I misunderstood then.

I pushed a commit that sets the `FT_` values for fields to their biggest size instead of their smallest.

A lot of the duplicate `unknown` fields are because we haven't reversed those yet and I doubt we'd want a billion fields called `unknown1`, `unknown2`, etc. So they are all semantically different fields despite them sharing the same field in Wireshark.

Several other fields like `guid` and `flags` share a similar dual purpose.
